title: Percentage
summary: The language of the whole arithmetic section — profit-loss, interest, discount and DI are all percentage questions in disguise. Tier 1 asks 1–2 direct questions per shift (successive change, more/less flips, election and population problems) and Tier 2 leans on it heavily.

subtopics.title: Percentage meaning & conversions
subtopics.concept:
Per cent means per hundred: $x\% = \frac{x}{100}$. The single most profitable memorisation in Quant is the fraction table — every CGL percentage, profit-loss, interest and DI question gets faster.

| Fraction | % | Fraction | % |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\frac{1}{2}$ | 50% | $\frac{1}{8}$ | 12.5% |
| $\frac{1}{3}$ | $33\frac{1}{3}\%$ | $\frac{3}{8}$ | 37.5% |
| $\frac{2}{3}$ | $66\frac{2}{3}\%$ | $\frac{5}{8}$ | 62.5% |
| $\frac{1}{4}$ | 25% | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $16\frac{2}{3}\%$ |
| $\frac{3}{4}$ | 75% | $\frac{5}{6}$ | $83\frac{1}{3}\%$ |
| $\frac{1}{5}$ | 20% | $\frac{1}{7}$ | $14\frac{2}{7}\%$ |
| $\frac{2}{5}$ | 40% | $\frac{1}{9}$ | $11\frac{1}{9}\%$ |
| $\frac{1}{12}$ | $8\frac{1}{3}\%$ | $\frac{1}{16}$ | 6.25% |

**Handy symmetry:** $x\%$ of $y = y\%$ of $x$ (16% of 25 = 25% of 16).

$p\%$ of a quantity $N = \frac{pN}{100}$; to find the whole when a part is known, divide: $N = \frac{\text{part} \times 100}{p}$.

formulas.name: Commutativity
formulas.tex: x\% \text{ of } y = y\% \text{ of } x

tricks.title: The fraction table IS the shortcut
tricks.body: Convert percentages to fractions before multiplying: 12.5% of 640 = 1/8 × 640 = 80. One line, no calculator.

tricks.title: Swap the percentages
tricks.body: Use $x\%$ of $y = y\%$ of $x$ when the swapped pair is friendlier.

example.q: Find 4% of 25.

tricks.title: Part-to-whole in one division
tricks.body: 'p% of a number is k' ⇒ number = 100k/p. Look at options: only one will make the product land on k.

example.q: If 40% of a number is 256, find the number.

mistakes: Treating $x\%$ of $y$ as $xy$ (missing the ÷100).
Converting 1/8 as 18% instead of 12.5%.
Dividing by the wrong base: % change must always use the ORIGINAL value as denominator.
Reading 'B's income is x% of A's' as 'x% more than A's'.
subtopics.notes:
### What does "per cent" mean?
Per cent means **out of hundred**: $x\% = \frac{x}{100}$. So 35% of a quantity means 35 parts out of every 100 parts of it: $35\% \text{ of } N = \frac{35N}{100}$.
Percentages let us compare unlike totals: 36/60 in one test and 45/75 in another are both 60% — instantly comparable.

### The fraction table (memorise cold — it pays for the whole topic)
| Fraction | % | Fraction | % |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1/2 | 50% | 1/8 | 12.5% |
| 1/3 | $33\frac{1}{3}$% | 3/8 | 37.5% |
| 2/3 | $66\frac{2}{3}$% | 1/6 | $16\frac{2}{3}$% |
| 1/4 | 25% | 5/6 | $83\frac{1}{3}$% |
| 3/4 | 75% | 1/7 | $14\frac{2}{7}$% |
| 1/5 | 20% | 1/9 | $11\frac{1}{9}$% |
| 2/5 | 40% | 1/12 | $8\frac{1}{3}$% |
| 5/8 | 62.5% | 1/16 | 6.25% |

### Four moves that answer every basic question
1. **x% of N** → fraction × N. $12.5\%$ of 960 $= \frac{1}{8} \times 960 = 120$.
2. **Recover the whole** from a part: if $p\%$ of N is k, then $N = \frac{100k}{p}$. 35% of N is 189 → $N = \frac{189 \times 100}{35} = 540$.
3. **One quantity as a % of another**: $\frac{A}{B} \times 100$. 45 out of 360 → $\frac{45}{360} \times 100 = 12.5\%$. The base sits right after the words "of" or "out of".
4. **Swap trick**: $x\%$ of $y = y\%$ of $x$. $4\%$ of 25 $= 25\%$ of 4 $= 1$.

### Chained percentages on the same base
$35\%$ of N $+ 45\%$ of N $= 80\%$ of N — add the percentages first when the base is the same. The same works for subtraction: "spent 30% on rent and 25% on food → 55% gone, 45% left."
But successive changes of the same quantity do **not** add — that is a different (and famous) trap covered in the increase/decrease subtopic.

### Using the unit-percent
1% of N is N ÷ 100. Build any percentage from tens and ones: 24% of 650 → 10% is 65, so 24% = 2 × 65 + 4 × 6.5 = 130 + 26 = 156. This mental decomposition is faster than any written multiplication.
The same idea runs in reverse: "what % is 78 of 650?" → 78 ÷ 6.5 = 12%.

### Percentages in everyday exam language
"60% of the students are boys" → 40% are girls, and any part = total × fraction. If 35% of the class are girls and there are 21 girls, the class size = 21 × 100/35 = 60. The exam always keeps totals whole, so a fractional total is a free signal that your arithmetic slipped.
Discount is a percentage of the marked price, and tax in these questions is simply added on the reduced amount afterwards.

### Where the base sits
"A is 20% of B" → B is the base. "What % of B is A?" → base is B again. Exam favourite: a fall from ₹250 to ₹200 is a 20% fall (base 250), but rising back from ₹200 to ₹250 is a 25% rise (base 200) — same ₹50, different base.

### Quick revision
- $x\% = \frac{x}{100}$; the fraction table is the speed key.
- Part → whole: $N = \frac{100k}{p}$.
- "What % of": divide by the base, × 100.
- $x\%$ of $y = y\%$ of $x$.
- Same base → add/subtract the percentages directly.

patterns.name: Find x% of a number (fraction table)
patterns.howToSpot: 'What is 24% of 650?' or 'find $12\frac{1}{2}$% of 960' — a direct percentage of a given number.
patterns.logic:
1. Replace x% by its table fraction (12.5% → 1/8, 16⅔% → 1/6 …).
2. Divide N by the denominator, multiply by the numerator.
3. For ugly percentages, build them from 10% and 1% of N.

Why: percentages are fractions with a fixed denominator — the table just gives friendlier denominators.

patterns.name: Recover the base, then apply another percentage
patterns.howToSpot: 'If 35% of a number is 189, find 80% of it' — a part is given, a different part is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Recover the whole: $N = \frac{\text{part} \times 100}{p}$.
2. Take the asked percentage of N.
3. Shortcut: find 1% of N (k ÷ p) and scale — 1% × 80 gives 80% directly.

Why: both parts are fixed fractions of the same whole, so the whole unlocks every other part.

example.q: If 35% of a number is 189, what is 80% of that number?

patterns.name: Fraction ↔ percentage conversion
patterns.howToSpot: 'Express 5/16 as a percentage' or 'write 87.5% as a fraction' — pure conversion, both directions.
patterns.logic:
1. Fraction → %: multiply by 100 (equivalently, scale the table value: 1/8 = 12.5% → 5/8 = 62.5%).
2. % → fraction: put x over 100, reduce. Use the table in reverse for standard values.
3. Decimals shift two places: 0.375 = 37.5%.

Why: 'per cent' is just a denominator of 100; conversion moves the number across that fixed denominator.

example.q: Express $\frac{5}{16}$ as a percentage.

patterns.name: One quantity as a percentage of another
patterns.howToSpot: '45 is what per cent of 360?' / 'A's income is what % of B's?' — two quantities, the base named after 'of'.
patterns.logic:
1. Identify the base (the value after 'of').
2. Divide the part by the base, multiply by 100.
3. Comparative version: 'A is x% and B is y% more than C' → A is $\frac{100 + x}{100 + y} \times 100\%$ of B.

Why: a percentage always needs a base; the question names it with 'of'.

example.q: Two numbers are respectively 20% and 50% more than a third number. The first number is what per cent of the second?
example.solution: Let the third number be 100 → numbers 120 and 150. $\frac{120}{150} \times 100 = 80\%$.

subtopics.title: Percentage increase / decrease & successive change
subtopics.concept:
Percentage change $= \frac{\text{final} - \text{initial}}{\text{initial}} \times 100$ (initial = the base being changed).

**Two successive changes** of $a\%$ and $b\%$ combine to $a + b + \frac{ab}{100}$ (keep minus signs for decreases).

+10% then −10% is **not** zero: net $= -\frac{10^2}{100} = -1\%$ (a fall of a²/100 %).

To restore an original value after a multiplier, divide back: if $F = I \times \frac{120}{100}$ then $I = F \times \frac{100}{120}$.

Model every change as a fraction multiplier: +20% → ×6/5, −25% → ×3/4. Chain the multipliers.

formulas.name: Successive change
formulas.note: use signs: + for increase, − for decrease

tricks.title: Multiplier chaining
tricks.body: Replace every % by its fraction multiplier and multiply across all steps.

example.q: A number is increased by 20% and the result is decreased by 10%. Net change?

tricks.title: a + b + ab/100 in one line
tricks.body: Add, then adjust by the product term. Fastest when one change is small.

example.q: Successive changes: +30% and −20%.

tricks.title: Reverse to the original
tricks.body: To undo +25%, divide by 5/4 (not multiply by 75/100).

example.q: After a 25% increase a salary is ₹50,000. What was it before?

mistakes: Adding successive percentages without the $\frac{ab}{100}$ term.
Assuming +x% followed by −x% is a net zero.
Using the new (increased) value as the base when computing a percentage decrease.
Undoing +25% by applying −25% (the right move is ÷1.25).
subtopics.notes:
### Percentage change and its base
$$\%\ \text{change} = \frac{\text{final} - \text{initial}}{\text{initial}} \times 100$$
The denominator is the value **before** the change. ₹250 → ₹200 is a fall of $\frac{50}{250} = 20\%$; going back from ₹200 to ₹250 is a rise of $\frac{50}{200} = 25\%$. Same ₹50, different base, different percentage.

### The multiplier ("chip") idea — the master shortcut
Every change is a chip: $+20\% \to \times\frac{6}{5}$, $-25\% \to \times\frac{3}{4}$, $+8\% \to \times\frac{27}{25}$.
**Forward:** multiply the chips. **Backward:** divide by them.
Example: $+20\%$ then $-10\%$: $\frac{6}{5} \times \frac{9}{10} = \frac{27}{25}$ → net $+8\%$.
Example: two $-10\%$ steps leave 8100 → before: $8100 \times \frac{10}{9} \times \frac{10}{9} = 10000$.

### Two successive changes: $a + b + \frac{ab}{100}$
Keep the signs: $+30\%$ then $-20\%$: $30 - 20 - \frac{600}{100} = +4\%$. Both increases: $+15\%$ then $+12\%$: $15 + 12 + 1.8 = +28.8\%$.
Works only for exactly two changes; for three or more, chain the chips.

### The round-trip rule: $+x\%$ and $-x\%$ never cancel
Same size up then down (either order): net $= -\frac{x^2}{100}\%$.
$+20\%$ then $-20\%$: net $-4\%$. A fall of 25% then a rise of 25%: net $-6.25\%$. The percentage always lands a little **below** the start — remember this to kill "no change" options at sight.

### Numerator–denominator changes
If the numerator changes by $a\%$ and the denominator by $b\%$, the fraction's chip is $\frac{100 + a}{100 + b}$ (a ratio of chips):
numerator $+50\%$, denominator $-25\%$: $\frac{150}{100} \div \frac{75}{100} = 2$ → the fraction doubles ($+100\%$).

### Restoring the original value
To undo $+25\%$, **divide** by $\frac{5}{4}$ — do not apply $-25\%$. A salary of ₹50,000 after a 25% rise was $50000 \times \frac{4}{5} = ₹40{,}000$ before. Applying $-25\%$ gives 37,500 — the classic wrong answer.
Same for cuts: after a $12.5\%$ cut a price is ₹3,500 → original $= 3500 \div \frac{7}{8} = ₹4{,}000$.

### How the questions are dressed up
The same five ideas arrive as prices, salaries, output of a factory, exam scores, or the value of a share — the chips do not care about the story. Two changes in the wording ("and then", "subsequently", "after some months") always means successive; a single change with two numbers (from A to B) is a plain c1. The options are built from classic slips: wrong base in the change %, subtracting instead of dividing to undo, and "no change" for the round trip.

### Quick revision
- % change: base is the value before the change.
- Chips: multiply forward, divide backward.
- Two changes: $a + b + \frac{ab}{100}$ with signs.
- $+x\%$ and $-x\%$ in any order → net $-\frac{x^2}{100}\%$.
- Undo a change with the reciprocal chip, never the opposite percentage.

patterns.name: Single percentage increase or decrease
patterns.howToSpot: A value moves from A to B and the % change is asked — price, population, marks, anything.
patterns.logic:
1. Compute the absolute change (final − initial).
2. Divide by the INITIAL value — the one before the change.
3. Multiply by 100; sign tells the direction.

Why: a percentage change always measures the movement against where the value started.

example.q: The salary of an employee rises from ₹18,000 to ₹20,700. Find the percentage increase.

patterns.name: Two successive changes (net change)
patterns.howToSpot: 'Increased by a% and then decreased by b% — net change?' Often dressed as price, value or output.
patterns.logic:
1. Apply $a + b + \frac{ab}{100}$ with the signs of the two changes.
2. Or multiply the chips ($\frac{100+a}{100} \times \frac{100+b}{100}$) and read the net.
3. The chip method is safe for any number of changes.

Why: the second change acts on the changed value, and the $\frac{ab}{100}$ term is exactly that correction.

example.q: A number is increased by 15% and then decreased by 12%. The net change is:

patterns.name: Same % up and down (round trip)
patterns.howToSpot: 'The price rises x% and then falls x%' (or falls then rises) — a guaranteed 'no change' trap among the options.
patterns.logic:
1. Write the net change as $-\frac{x^2}{100}\%$ — order does not matter.
2. Or verify with chips: $\frac{120}{100} \times \frac{80}{100} = \frac{24}{25} = 0.96$ → $-4\%$.
3. The final value is always BELOW the start (for any x > 0).

Why: the second change works on a bigger or smaller base, so the absolute swings differ.

example.q: The price of a commodity first rises by 20% and then falls by 20%. The net change in price is:

patterns.name: Restore the original value (work backwards)
patterns.howToSpot: The value AFTER the change(s) is given and the original is asked: 'after a 20% increase the population is 8,400…'.
patterns.logic:
1. Write the chip of each change.
2. Divide the final value by the chips (or multiply by their reciprocals).
3. Never 'apply the opposite percentage' — that uses the wrong base.

Why: forward = multiply by chips, so backward = divide by the same chips.

example.q: After successive decreases of 10% and 20%, a number becomes 720. Find the number.

patterns.name: Fraction changes: numerator and denominator move
patterns.howToSpot: 'The numerator is increased by 20% and the denominator decreased by 10% — the fraction becomes?'
patterns.logic:
1. Write the chip of the numerator and of the denominator.
2. Divide the numerator chip by the denominator chip — that is the fraction's new factor.
3. Factor − 1 is the percentage change of the fraction.

Why: the fraction scales by (numerator chip)/(denominator chip), since denominator changes divide.

example.q: The numerator of a fraction is increased by 50% and the denominator is decreased by 25%. The fraction becomes:
example.solution: Chips: $\frac{3}{2}$ and $\frac{3}{4}$ → factor $= \frac{3}{2} \div \frac{3}{4} = 2$ → the fraction is doubled ($+100\%$).

subtopics.title: 'x% more than' ↔ 'x% less than' & chains
subtopics.concept:
The 'more than / less than' pair has **different bases** — this asymmetry is tested constantly.

- If A is $x\%$ **more** than B: $A = B\left(1 + \frac{x}{100}\right)$, and B is $\frac{100x}{100 + x}\%$ **less** than A.
- If A is $x\%$ **less** than B: $A = B\left(1 - \frac{x}{100}\right)$, and B is $\frac{100x}{100 - x}\%$ **more** than A.

**Chains:** if A = a% of B and B = b% of C, then A $= \frac{ab}{100}\%$ of C.

The 'less than' percentage is always LARGER than the 'more than' percentage — use that to sanity-check options.

formulas.name: Less → more
formulas.tex: A = B\left(1 - \frac{x}{100}\right) \Rightarrow \text{B is } \frac{100x}{100-x}\% \text{ more than A}

tricks.title: Flip with 100x/(100±x)
tricks.body: More→less uses 100+x in the denominator; less→more uses 100−x. The answer must be bigger than x for the less→more direction.

example.q: A's salary is 25% more than B's. B's salary is what per cent less than A's?

tricks.title: Assume the base = 100
tricks.body: Set the unmentioned quantity to 100 and read off both values.

example.q: A's salary is 20% more than B's. By what per cent is B's salary less than A's?

tricks.title: Chain percentages by multiplying fractions
tricks.body: Convert each link to a fraction of the next and multiply.

example.q: A's income is 40% of B's, and B's is 25% of C's. A's income is what % of C's?

mistakes: Answering 'x% less' with the same x (the correct value $\frac{100x}{100+x}$ is always smaller than x).
Using 100 − x in the denominator for the more→less direction.
Chaining by adding percentages instead of multiplying fractions.
Ignoring which quantity the question calls the base.
subtopics.notes:
### The base decides everything
"A is x% more than B" uses **B** as the base; "B is ?% less than A" uses **A** as the base. Different denominators → different percentages. From 100 to 125 is $+25\%$, but from 125 back to 100 is $-20\%$ — a 25% rise is undone by a 20% fall, never by a 25% fall.

### The flip formulas
$$\text{More} \to \text{less}: \frac{100x}{100 + x}\%, \qquad \text{Less} \to \text{more}: \frac{100x}{100 - x}\%$$
Standard pairs to memorise: 25% more ↔ 20% less; 20% less ↔ 25% more; 50% more ↔ $33\frac{1}{3}$% less; 20% more ↔ $16\frac{2}{3}$% less.
Sanity check that kills wrong options: the "less" answer is always **smaller** than x, the "more" answer is always **bigger** than x.

### Assume the base = 100
The bullet-proof method: set the unmentioned quantity to 100, compute both values, then compute the asked percentage on its own base.
Example: A is 60% more than B → B = 100, A = 160 → B is $\frac{60}{160} \times 100 = 37.5\%$ less than A.
This also handles the recovery version: production falls from 1,500 to 1,200 → to regain 1,500 it must now rise by $\frac{300}{1200} \times 100 = 25\%$, not 20% — the base shrank, so the recovery percentage is always **bigger** than the fall.

### Chains of percentages
A = 30% of B and B = 40% of C → $A = \frac{30}{100} \times \frac{40}{100} \times C = 12\%$ of C. **Multiply** the fractions — never add.
Workplace version: 40% of the employees are graduates and 25% of the graduates are post-graduates → post-graduates $= \frac{40}{100} \times \frac{25}{100} = 10\%$ of all employees. The two percentages sit on different totals, so they chain.

### How the examiner flips the wording
Same arithmetic, four costumes:
- "A's salary is 25% more than B's" ↔ "B's salary is 20% less than A's".
- "A is heavier than B by 25%..." — weight of B is the base.
- "If A's income is 25% more than B's, B's income is less than A's by what %?" — the classic flip.
- "The marks of A are 20% less than B" → A/B = 4/5, so B is $\frac{1}{4}$ more = 25% more. Convert to the ratio A : B = 80 : 100 whenever the wording tangles you.

### Speed pairs worth memorising
| "more than" | equals "less than" (the other way) |
|---|---|
| 25% more | 20% less |
| $33\frac{1}{3}$% more | 25% less |
| 50% more | $33\frac{1}{3}$% less |
| $66\frac{2}{3}$% more | 40% less |
| 100% more | 50% less |
Reading the table right to left covers the "less → more" questions too.

### Quick revision
- More→less: $\frac{100x}{100 + x}$. Less→more: $\frac{100x}{100 - x}$.
- Base = 100 solves every variant, including chained ones.
- Chains: multiply fractions of successive bases.
- Recovery % > fall %; "less" answer < x < "more" answer.

patterns.name: 'More than' flipped to 'less than'
patterns.howToSpot: 'A's income is x% more than B's — B's income is what % less than A's?' The base changes mid-question.
patterns.logic:
1. Flip formula: $\frac{100x}{100 + x}\%$ less.
2. Or set B = 100 → A = 100 + x; the gap x sits on base (100 + x).
3. Ratio route: A : B = (100 + x) : 100; less % = excess/base × 100.

Why: the same gap is x% of B but a smaller % of the bigger A.

example.q: A's income is 60% more than B's. B's income is what per cent less than A's?

patterns.name: 'Less than' flipped to 'more than'
patterns.howToSpot: 'B is x% less than A — A is what % more than B?' Also appears as 'by what % must it rise to get back?'
patterns.logic:
1. Flip formula: $\frac{100x}{100 - x}\%$ more.
2. Or set A = 100 → B = 100 − x; the gap x sits on the smaller base (100 − x).
3. Recovery version: fall from F to N → rise needed $= \frac{F - N}{N} \times 100\%$ — base is the reduced value.

Why: after a fall the base is smaller, so the matching rise is always the bigger number.

example.q: The production of a factory falls from 1,500 units to 1,200 units. By what per cent must it now increase to reach 1,500 units again?
example.solution: Gap $= 300$ on the reduced base 1,200 → $\frac{300}{1200} \times 100 = 25\%$. (Not 20% — that would undo it on the old base.)

patterns.name: Chained percentages (A is a% of B, B is b% of C)
patterns.howToSpot: '40% of the employees are graduates, 25% of the graduates are post-graduates' — a percentage of a percentage.
patterns.logic:
1. Write each statement as a fraction of its own base.
2. Multiply the fractions: $\frac{a}{100} \times \frac{b}{100} \times C$.
3. Read A as $\frac{ab}{100}\%$ of the outermost base C.

Why: each percentage sits on a different total, so they compose multiplicatively — the same logic as successive discounts.

example.q: In an office, 40% of the employees are graduates and 25% of the graduates are post-graduates. Post-graduates form what per cent of all employees?
example.solution: $\frac{40}{100} \times \frac{25}{100} = \frac{10}{100}$ → 10% of all employees. (Adding 40 + 25 = 65% is the trap.)

patterns.name: Two quantities compared through a common base
patterns.howToSpot: 'A is x% more than C and B is y% more than C — A is what % of B?' Both percentages sit on the same hidden base.
patterns.formula: A : B = (100 + x) : (100 + y) \ \Rightarrow\ \frac{A}{B} = \frac{100 + x}{100 + y} \times 100\%
patterns.logic:
1. Set the common base C = 100.
2. A = 100 + x and B = 100 + y.
3. The asked ratio is A/B × 100 — one division.

Why: a shared base turns two independent percentages into one ratio.

example.q: A's height is 50% more than C's, and B's height is 20% more than C's. B's height is what per cent of A's height?

subtopics.title: Population growth, depreciation & elections
subtopics.concept:
**Population / value growth-decay:** value after n years $= P\left(1 \pm \frac{r}{100}\right)^n$ (+ for growth, − for depreciation). Work backwards by dividing.

**Two different rates** in two years: apply the multipliers one after another (e.g. ×11/10 then ×19/20).

**Election problems:** total votes polled = valid + invalid. Both candidates' shares must be read off the VALID votes. Margin = difference of shares × valid votes.

Depreciation is the same formula with a negative rate: present $= P\left(\frac{100-r}{100}\right)^n$.

tricks.title: Multiplier chips for n years
tricks.body: Chips: +10% → 11/10, −5% → 19/20. Multiply chips across years; the final fraction tells everything.

example.q: A town's population of 40,000 grows 10% in year 1 and falls 5% in year 2. Find the present population.

tricks.title: Work backwards with division
tricks.body: For 'value n years ago', divide by the chips instead of guessing.

example.q: A machine worth ₹8,100 depreciates at 10% p.a. What was its value 2 years ago?
example.solution: Divide by the chip twice: ₹$8100 \times \frac{10}{9} = 9000$, then $9000 \times \frac{10}{9} = 10000$.

tricks.title: Elections: everything on valid votes
tricks.body: Convert both candidates' data to fractions of valid votes; the total polled number then follows from the margin.

example.q: In an election, 20% of votes polled were invalid. The winner got 60% of valid votes and won by 1200 votes. Total votes polled?
example.solution: Margin = 20% of valid = $\frac{1}{5}V = 1200$ ⇒ V = 6000 = 80% of total ⇒ total = 7500.

mistakes: Applying $\left(1 + \frac{r}{100}\right)^n$ when the two years have different rates.
Counting invalid votes as a candidate's votes.
Depreciating 2 years as $P - 2r\%$ instead of $\left(\frac{90}{100}\right)^2$.
In 'population 2 years ago' questions, dividing by (1 + net%) with the averaged rate.
subtopics.notes:
### Growth and depreciation over years
Value after n years at r% per annum: $P\left(1 \pm \frac{r}{100}\right)^n$ — plus for growth, minus for depreciation.
Different rates in different years: multiply the chips one after another; never average the rates.
Example: 40,000 → +10% then −5%: $40000 \times \frac{11}{10} \times \frac{19}{20} = 41{,}800$.
Handy exact chips: 10% → $\frac{11}{10}$ or $\frac{9}{10}$; 20% → $\frac{6}{5}$; 25% → $\frac{5}{4}$; 5% → $\frac{21}{20}$; 12.5% → $\frac{9}{8}$ or $\frac{7}{8}$.

### Backwards questions (present given, past asked)
Present = P × chip¹ × chip² …, so divide by the chips to go back.
Example: a machine is worth ₹8,100 after two yearly depreciations of 10%: $8100 \div \frac{9}{10} \div \frac{9}{10} = ₹10{,}000$.
Do **not** divide by the net change (1 − 20% ≠ 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81).

### Watch the walk-through with P = 100
For any multi-year story, take the starting value as 100 and track it year by year:
+10% then −5% then +20%: $100 \to 110 \to 104.5 \to 125.4$ — the final value is 125.4% of the start, a net +25.4%.
This kills every option at a glance and needs no formula at all. When the answer choices are far apart (they usually are), even rough chips decide the question: "is it above or below 41,000?" is enough.

### Elections — the two golden rules
1. Every candidate's share is a percentage of the **valid** votes, never of the total polled.
2. Margin = (winner% − loser%) × valid votes.
With invalid votes, chain once more: valid = (100 − invalid%) of the polled.
Example: 20% of the polled votes are invalid, the winner polls 60% of the valid votes and wins by 1,200 → margin = 20% of valid → valid = 6,000 = 80% of polled → polled = 7,500.

### One-candidate and turnout variants
- "x% did not vote / their votes were invalid" → handle the turnout first, then split the rest.
- A candidate who withdraws: subtract that share before splitting between the remaining two.
- "Winner got 55% of the total votes (no invalid votes)": margin = (2 × 55 − 100)% = 10% of the votes.

### Depreciation nuance
"Depreciates 10% p.a. for 2 years" is $\left(\frac{9}{10}\right)^2 = 0.81$ — a total fall of **19%**, not 20%. The "20%" option is always planted.

### Elections — one more worked shape
"A candidate got 30% of the total valid votes and lost by 4,000": the winner has 70%, so the margin is 40% of the valid votes → valid $= \frac{4000 \times 100}{40} = 10{,}000$ and the loser's votes $= 3{,}000$. Everything again reduces to one equation on valid votes. If the question instead names "total voters on the roll" with a turnout of 80%, the valid votes sit inside the turnout: roll → turnout → valid → shares, left to right, one chip each.

### Quick revision
- $P_n = P \times \text{chip}^n$; chips multiply; go back by dividing.
- Different rates → different chips, applied in order.
- Elections: everything sits on valid votes; margin = share gap × valid.
- $\left(1 - \frac{r}{100}\right)^2 \ne 1 - \frac{2r}{100}$.

patterns.name: Population growth over n years
patterns.howToSpot: 'A town's population is P and increases at r% per annum — population after n years?'
patterns.logic:
1. Write the chip $\frac{100 + r}{100}$.
2. Multiply P by chipⁿ (or apply chip n times).
3. Two different rates in two years → multiply the two different chips.

Why: each year's growth sits on the grown value, so the changes compound multiplicatively.

example.q: The population of a town is 6,400 and increases at 25% per annum. What will it be after 2 years?

patterns.name: Backwards: present value → past value / depreciation
patterns.howToSpot: 'The present population is X; it grew at r% p.a. — find the population n years ago' or 'a machine worth M depreciates at r% p.a. — value after n years'.
patterns.logic:
1. Forward: multiply by the depreciation chipⁿ.
2. Backward: divide the present value by the growth chipⁿ — never divide by the net %.
3. Check the answer by growing it forward once.

Why: compounding is not symmetric — undo a 25% rise with ÷(5/4), not with −25%.

example.q: The present population of a town is 16,000. If it has been growing at 25% per annum, what was its population 2 years ago?

patterns.name: Two different rates in consecutive years
patterns.howToSpot: 'Increases by 10% in the first year and decreases by 5% in the second' — rates differ or a sign flips.
patterns.logic:
1. One chip per year, signs included: +5% → 21/20, −10% → 9/10.
2. Multiply the chips in order (or take P = 100 and walk through).
3. For 'what was it 3 years ago', divide by all three chips.

Why: each year's rate applies to the value left by the previous year.

example.q: The population of a town is 80,000. It increases by 5% in the first year and decreases by 10% in the second year. What is the population at the end of the second year?

patterns.name: Election with valid/invalid votes and margin
patterns.howToSpot: 'In an election, x% of the votes were invalid; the winner got y% of the valid votes and won by M votes.'
patterns.logic:
1. Chain: polled → valid (drop the invalid %) → shares of the winner and loser.
2. Margin = share gap × valid votes; equate it to the given margin.
3. Two candidates: L = 100 − W (on valid votes).

Why: candidates' percentages are defined on valid votes, so every equation must sit on that base.

example.q: In an election between two candidates, 20% of the votes polled were invalid. The winner got 60% of the valid votes and won by 1,200 votes. How many votes were polled in all?
example.solution: Valid = 0.8 × polled; margin = 20% of valid = 1200 → valid = 6000 → polled = $\frac{6000}{0.8} = 7{,}500$.

subtopics.title: Marks, income–expenditure–savings & price–consumption
subtopics.concept:
**Pass-marks template:** candidate 1 scores $p\%$ and fails by $f$ marks ⇒ pass mark $= \frac{pM}{100} + f$; candidate 2 scores $q\%$ and exceeds by $e$ ⇒ pass mark $= \frac{qM}{100} - e$. Equate and solve for maximum marks $M$.

**Income–expenditure:** savings = income − expenditure. If income is I and savings s%, expenditure = (100 − s)% of I.

**Price rises, keep expenditure fixed:** consumption must fall by $\frac{100r}{100 + r}\%$.
**Price falls, same quantity-money:** extra quantity bought $= \frac{\text{money} \times r}{100 \times \text{reduced price}}$; reduced price $= \frac{r\% \text{ of outlay}}{\text{extra quantity}}$.

formulas.name: Price cut & extra quantity
formulas.tex: \text{reduced price} = \frac{r\% \text{ of outlay}}{\text{extra quantity}},\quad \text{old price} = \frac{\text{reduced price}}{1 - r/100}

tricks.title: Marks gap = percentage gap
tricks.body: In two-candidate mark problems the difference of the two percentages times M equals the total mark gap (fail-by + exceed-by).

example.q: A candidate scoring 33% fails by 45 marks; another scoring 45% gets 15 marks more than the pass mark. Find the maximum marks.

tricks.title: Income = 100 bookkeeping
tricks.body: Set income to 100, express savings and expenditure, then apply every change and read the answer off.

example.q: A man saves 20% of his income. His income rises 15% and expenditure rises 10%. % increase in savings?
example.solution: Income 100 → save 20, spend 80. New: income 115, spend 88 ⇒ save 27. Increase = 7/20 = 35%.

tricks.title: Price cut: r% of money buys the extra
tricks.body: A r% price cut saves r% of the outlay, and that saved money buys the extra quantity at the REDUCED price.

example.q: A 20% cut in sugar price lets a buyer get 5 kg more for ₹400. Find the original price.
example.solution: Saved money = 20% of 400 = ₹80 = price of extra 5 kg ⇒ reduced price ₹16/kg ⇒ original price = ₹$16 \times \frac{100}{80}$ = ₹20 per kg.

mistakes: Using the fail-by and exceed-by marks with the same sign (they act in opposite directions: +f and −e on the two sides).
In savings problems, raising expenditure by 10% as 'reduce savings by 10%'.
For the price-cut question, dividing the full outlay (not r% of it) by the extra quantity.
Consumption reduction for a 25% price rise answered as 25% instead of 20%.
subtopics.notes:
### Pass-marks problems
The pass mark is one fixed number seen from two candidates:
- A scores p% and **fails by** f marks → pass $= \frac{pM}{100} + f$.
- B scores q% and scores **e marks more than** the pass mark → pass $= \frac{qM}{100} - e$.
Equate the two: $\frac{(q - p)M}{100} = f + e$ → find M, then the pass mark.
Example: 33% fails by 45, 45% exceeds by 15 → 12% of M = 60 → M = 500, pass = 210.
Signs matter: fail-by pushes the pass mark **up** from the score, exceeds-by pulls it **down**.
Single-candidate version: if the pass mark is given directly, $\frac{pM}{100} + f = \text{pass}$ → M.

### Income–expenditure–savings bookkeeping
savings = income − expenditure. Set **income = 100** and all three numbers stay visible.
Example: spends 80% of income; income rises 15%, expenditure rises 10%:
$100/80/20 \to 115/88/27$ → savings rise $\frac{7}{20} \times 100 = 35\%$.
The percentage change in savings is almost never equal to the change in income — always recompute the new savings. If a person saves s% of income, expenditure is (100 − s)% of it.

### Price vs consumption
expenditure = price × quantity, so quantity chip = expenditure chip ÷ price chip.
- Price +25%, expenditure unchanged → quantity chip $= 1 \div \frac{5}{4} = \frac{4}{5}$ → cut 20%. (Standard formula: cut $= \frac{100r}{100 + r}\%$.)
- Price +20%, expenditure allowed to rise 8% → chip $= \frac{108}{120} = 0.9$ → cut 10%.
- Price +40%, consumption cut 25% → expenditure chip $= 1.4 \times 0.75 = 1.05$ → +5%.
Never equate the consumption cut to the price rise — they are related by division, not equality.

### Price cut with extra quantity
A price cut of r% on an outlay M saves r% of M; the saving buys the **extra** quantity at the reduced price.
reduced price = (r% of M) ÷ extra quantity → original price = reduced ÷ (1 − r/100).
Example: a 20% cut lets a family buy 5 kg more for ₹400 → saved = ₹80 → reduced price = 16/kg → original $= 16 \times \frac{5}{4} = ₹20$.

### Exam traps
- Fail-by and exceed-by act in opposite directions (+f, −e); a same-sign slip ruins M.
- Savings % change ≠ income % change; compute the new savings from scratch.
- Consumption cut ≠ price rise (20% ≠ 25%): divide the chips.
- Depreciation/price-cut chains: work in chips, not in added percentages.

### Quick revision
- $\frac{(q - p)M}{100} = f + e$ for two candidates.
- Income = 100 bookkeeping solves every savings question.
- Quantity chip = expenditure chip ÷ price chip.
- An r% cut saves r% of the outlay → extra quantity at the reduced price.

patterns.name: Pass marks with two candidates
patterns.howToSpot: 'A candidate scoring p% fails by f marks; another scoring q% gets e marks more than the pass mark.'
patterns.formula: \frac{(q - p)M}{100} = f + e \ \Rightarrow\ M = \frac{100(f + e)}{q - p}
patterns.logic:
1. Write pass mark from each candidate: pM/100 + f and qM/100 − e.
2. Equate → (q − p)% of M = f + e → maximum marks M.
3. Pass mark = pM/100 + f (verify with the second candidate).

Why: both expressions equal the same pass mark; subtracting them cancels it and leaves M.

example.q: A candidate scoring 33% fails by 45 marks, while another scoring 45% gets 15 marks more than the pass marks. Find the maximum marks.

patterns.name: Income–expenditure–savings change
patterns.howToSpot: 'He spends 80% of his income; income rises a% and expenditure rises b% — % change in savings?'
patterns.logic:
1. Set income = 100; write expenditure and savings.
2. Apply the two % changes to income and expenditure separately.
3. New savings = new income − new expenditure; % change on the old savings.

Why: savings is a leftover, not a base — its % change must be computed, never guessed.

example.q: A person spends 80% of his income. His income increases by 15% and his expenditure increases by 10%. The percentage increase in his savings is:

patterns.name: Price rise vs consumption (expenditure target)
patterns.howToSpot: 'The price rises by r% — by what % must consumption be cut so the expenditure stays the same?' (Or the expenditure is allowed to move by s%.)
patterns.logic:
1. Write chips: price $\frac{100 + r}{100}$, expenditure $\frac{100 + s}{100}$ (s = 0 for 'same').
2. Quantity chip = expenditure chip ÷ price chip.
3. 1 − quantity chip is the cut.

Why: expenditure = price × quantity, so quantity adjusts by the ratio of the other two chips.

example.q: The price of petrol rises by 25%. By what per cent must a family reduce its consumption so that the expenditure on petrol remains the same?

patterns.name: Price cut → extra quantity for the same money
patterns.howToSpot: 'A reduction of r% in the price enables a family to buy k kg more for ₹M — find the (original/reduced) price.'
patterns.logic:
1. The r% cut saves r% of M — that saving is spent on the extra k units.
2. Reduced price = saving ÷ k.
3. Original price = reduced price ÷ (1 − r/100).

Why: the outlay is unchanged, so the money freed by the cut is exactly what buys the extra quantity.

example.q: A reduction of 20% in the price of cooking oil enables a family to buy 5 kg more for ₹400. The original price per kg is:

pyqPatterns.pattern: x% of a number / fraction conversion
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'What is 35% of 480', '1/8 as a percentage', 'if p% of N is k find N'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Fraction table + one multiplication or division; recover the whole with N = 100k/p. Under 30 seconds — never long-multiply.

example.q: What is 35% of 480?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two or three changes applied one after another (price/population/marks), asking net change or final value.
pyqPatterns.approach: Multiplier chips (×6/5, ×3/4 …) or a + b + ab/100 for two changes. Up-then-down by the same rate → net −x²/100%. Three changes: chain the chips.

example.q: The price of an article rises by 20% and then falls by 20%. What is the net change?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'A's income is 25% more than B's; B's income is what % less than A's?' — the base changes mid-question.
pyqPatterns.approach: Flip formulas: 100x/(100+x) (more→less) and 100x/(100−x) (less→more). Or set the unmentioned quantity to 100. Chains of percentages: multiply fractions.

example.q: A's income is 20% more than B's. B's income is what per cent less than A's?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Population grows or falls at stated yearly rates (same or different); find present, past, or future value.
pyqPatterns.approach: Chain the chips forward (×1.1, ×0.9 …); divide by them to go back. Two different rates: never average — multiply chips. (1 − r/100)² ≠ 1 − 2r/100.

example.q: The population of a town is 40,000. It increases by 10% in the first year and decreases by 5% in the second. Population at the end of the second year?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two candidates, invalid votes given, winner's share of valid votes and margin given; find total votes or votes got.
pyqPatterns.approach: Everything sits on VALID votes: valid = (100 − invalid)% of polled; margin = share gap × valid; then unmask the total.

example.q: In an election, 20% of the votes polled were invalid. The winner got 60% of the valid votes and won by 1,200 votes. How many votes were polled?
example.solution: Margin = 20% of valid → valid = 6,000 = 80% of polled → polled = 7,500.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: One candidate fails by f marks at p%, another exceeds pass by e at q%; find maximum marks or the pass mark.
pyqPatterns.approach: (q − p)% of M = f + e. Solve M, then pass mark = pM/100 + f; verify with the second candidate.

example.q: A candidate scoring 33% fails by 45 marks; another scoring 45% gets 15 marks more than the pass marks. Find the maximum marks.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Price rises 20%, by what % reduce consumption to keep expenditure same' or the reverse (k kg more for a fixed outlay).
pyqPatterns.approach: Quantity factor = expenditure factor ÷ price factor; standard cut = 100r/(100+r)%. Outlay version: r% of the money buys the extra quantity at the reduced price.

example.q: A 20% cut in the price of oil lets a family buy 5 kg more for ₹400. Find the original price per kg.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Savings % given; income and expenditure change by given %; find the % change in savings.
pyqPatterns.approach: Set income = 100, track all three quantities with chips, and compute the new savings directly — the % change in savings is never guessed.

example.q: A person spends 80% of his income. Income rises 15% and expenditure rises 10%. Find the % increase in savings.

solvedExamples.q: A number is first increased by 20% and then decreased by 10%. What is the net percentage change?
Find the value of $16\frac{2}{3}\%$ of 720 $+$ $33\frac{1}{3}\%$ of 450.
The price of an article is first increased by 10% and then decreased by 10%. What is the net change in price?
solvedExamples.solution:
Net $= 10 - 10 - \frac{10 \times 10}{100} = -1\%$.
A rise of 10% followed by a fall of 10% always leaves a **1% decrease**.

solvedExamples.q: A's salary is 25% more than B's salary. B's salary is what per cent less than A's salary?
The value of a machine depreciates at the rate of 10% per annum. If its present value is ₹8,100, what was its value 2 years ago?
solvedExamples.solution:
Let the value 2 years ago be P.
$P\left(\frac{90}{100}\right)^2 = 8100$
$P \times \frac{81}{100} = 8100$, so P = ₹10,000.

practice.solution:
Valid = 85% of polled. Winner 60%, loser 40% → margin = 20% of valid.

A person spends 80% of his income. His income increases by 15% and his expenditure increases by 10%. His savings increase by:
practice.solution:
Income = 100 → spends 80, saves 20.
New: income 115, expenditure 88 → savings 27.
Increase $= \frac{7}{20} \times 100 = 35\%$.

practice.q: Ravi saves 25% of his income. His income rises by 30% and his expenditure rises by 20%. His new savings are what per cent more than his earlier savings?
practice.solution:
Income = 100 → saves 25, spends 75.
New: income 130, expenditure 90 → savings 40.
Increase $= \frac{15}{25} \times 100 = 60\%$.
